title: Ashtpadi 20, salok: wandering, I came
hookLine: phirat phirat: wandering and wandering, I have come to Your refuge (Sukhmani 20)

cards: Phirat phirat. Say it out loud and it sounds like footsteps: phirat, phirat, phirat. It's the first word of the twentieth ashtpadi, and it means wandering, turning, going round and round.
A car circles a city at night, looking for an address. Left, then left again, back past the same gas station, the phone saying recalculating.
And then, finally, the right door, the porch light on, and someone saying come in. Today's salok is that moment of arrival.

teach.h: THE SALOK: I HAVE COME, I HAVE FALLEN.
teach.b: The salok has two lines. In paraphrase: wandering and wandering, O God, I have come, and fallen at Your sanctuary. This is Nanak's prayer, O God: attach me to Your devotion.

teach.h: PHIRAT PHIRAT: A WHOLE LIFE OF DETOURS.
teach.b: Gurbani often doubles a word to make it last: phirat phirat isn't one detour, it's a whole life of them. Some readers hear in it the long round of births and deaths, the soul turning through lifetime after lifetime.

Others hear the ordinary wandering of a single life: job to job, want to want, one more thing that was supposed to finally make it feel settled. The text holds both. Then the verb: aaiaa, I have come.
Not I have earned my way in, or I have found the answer. Just: I'm here. Then pariaa: I've fallen, or laid myself down, at Your saran, Your refuge.
It's the posture of someone too tired to keep standing. The last line is the request, and notice what it doesn't ask for: no proof the wandering was worth it, no prize at the end.
It asks: attach me to Your bhagti, Your devotion.
After nineteen ashtpadis of lists and pictures and warnings, the twentieth opens with no argument at all. Just a traveler at the door, and a request to stay.

how: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's twentieth ashtpadi begin with its salok, in which the seeker, after long wandering, comes to God's refuge and asks only to be joined to devotion.

o: a resting place at the end of a road
arriving home after a long trip

p: devotion, what the salok asks for

s: the salok ends by asking for a reward for the long journey
it asks only to be attached to God's devotion.
Gurbani often doubles a word to make it last
phirat phirat: not one detour, a whole life of them.
the salok says the seeker earned the way in
the seeker simply comes, and falls at the refuge.

games.q: after a long wandering, you reach the door. what does the twentieth salok ask for?
o: proof that the wandering was worth it.
to be attached to devotion, and kept here.
games.why: Nanak's prayer in the salok is simply: attach me to Your devotion. no argument, no prize, just a request to stay.

practice: Let yourself arrive where you are: feel your body settle into the chair or the floor as if you'd just walked a long way, and let the shoulders drop.
With each breath out, say silently, I have come, and when thoughts start wandering, notice the footsteps, phirat phirat, and come back. If you pray, rest in Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Phirat, wandering, going round and round: its salok, phirat phirat, the seeker arrives after long wandering at God's refuge and asks only to be kept in devotion.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: phirat, wandering, going round; doubled in the salok as phirat phirat.

carryVoice: Your line: I have come. No prize asked for, only to be kept near. Rest easy.
